lesson.title: Tutoyer & Vouvoyer
lesson.subtitle: Choosing tu vs vous as social verbs, and how on ('one/the man') became spoken French's everyday 'we'.

hook.title: Why French Turned 'tu' and 'vous' Into Action Verbs: tutoyer & vouvoyer
hook.content: French has two verbs just to name the social register choice: tutoyer ('to say tu to someone') and vouvoyer ('to say vous to someone')! When two colleagues become friends, one asks: On peut se tutoyer ? ('Can we use tu with each other?'). And notice that 'we' is expressed by on — the worn-down form of Latin homō ('man/one')!

footnotes.title: How Latin homō ('man') split into two French words: l'homme and on
footnotes.content: Stressed as a noun, Latin homō became l'homme ('the man'). Unstressed in front of a verb, it wore down to on (/ɔ̃/)!

pattern.title: On se tutoie ? ('Shall we use tu?') and On = Spoken 'We'
pattern.content: Use vous with strangers until invited to switch (On se tutoie ?), and use on + 3rd-person singular verb as your everyday spoken 'we'.
pattern.linguist_note: Grammaticalization of Latin nominative homō into the subject clitic on is unique to Gallo-Romance.
pattern.trap_note: Remember: even when on means 'we', its reflexive pronoun is se (On se tutoie) and its verb is singular (On va, On est)!

exercises.prompt: Match each social pronoun or verb with its meaning:

matching_pairs.german: Can we use 'tu' with each other?

exercises.target_answer: to address someone as 'tu', to address someone as 'vous', Can we use 'tu' with each other?, we (everyday speech) / one / people
exercises.meaning: tutoyer quelqu'un, vouvoyer quelqu'un, On peut se tutoyer ?, on (from Latin homo 'man')
exercises.explanation: tutoyer and vouvoyer name the social register choice directly.

exercises.prompt: The pronoun 'on' ('one / we') is the unstressed twin of which French noun meaning 'man' (from Latin homō)?
exercises.explanation: Latin nominative homō became unstressed on; accusative hominem became homme!

exercises.prompt: A new colleague smiles and asks 'On se tutoie ?' What are they inviting you to do?
exercises.meaning: se tutoyer = to address each other as 'tu'
exercises.explanation: On se tutoie ? is the classic French milestone of friendship.

exercises.idea: we are going to the café together (using everyday On va)
cues: We go to the café → On va au café + together → ensemble
exercises.meaning: We are going to the café together
exercises.explanation: On va replaces Nous allons in everyday conversation.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Ici, tout le monde se tutoie
exercises.target_answer: Ici, tout le monde se tutoie
exercises.meaning: Here, everyone uses 'tu' with each other
exercises.explanation: tout le monde ('everyone') is singular in French!
exercises.affirmation: You wrote tout le monde se tutoie cleanly.

summary.outcome: Understand tutoyer/vouvoyer and use on (the worn-down twin of homme) for everyday 'we'.

use_example.german: Au travail, on se tutoie tous.
use_example.english: At work, we all use 'tu' with each other.

summary.takeaway: Wait for 'On se tutoie ?' to switch from vous to tu — and use on for everyday 'we'.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([5051] Lieu & Direction: ici, là, tout droit): see how Tutoyer & Vouvoyer leads directly into Lieu & Direction: ici, là, tout droit.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "We are going to the café together" in French:
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "On va au café ensemble" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Tutoyer & Vouvoyer.

tu.etymology_derivation: Latin tū — the very word the King James Bible still whispers as thou. Point your lips; the vowel is not English's.

vous.etymology_derivation: Latin vōs 'you all' promoted to politeness — the same T–V ladder as German Sie and English's lost 'ye'.

on.context_translation: Shall we go to the café?
on.etymology_derivation: on is worn-down homme — 'the man says' became 'one says' became spoken French's everyday 'we'. The nasal vowel is the fossil.

nous.etymology_derivation: Latin nōs — English keeps the root in nostrum.

homme.etymology_derivation: Latin homō 'man' — the root of human, homicide, humus (of the earth). The H is written and never said.

aller.context_translation: I'm going to go to the café.
aller.etymology_derivation: Latin ambulāre 'to walk' → ambler → aller. To go is a stroll away — and the near future rides on it.

ami.etymology_derivation: In liaison, un ami sounds like /œ̃.na.mi/ and mes amis like /me.za.mi/.
